title: An envelope and decay with time constants: how fast does it relax?
summary: A ringing signal drawn inside its decaying envelope, with markers at one, two and three time constants. The time constant tau turns 'how fast' into a number you can read off the axis.

media.alt: A teal oscillation shrinking with time inside two dashed amber envelope curves exp(-t/tau) and minus exp(-t/tau), with pink markers and dotted drop lines at t = 1.5, 3.0 and 4.5 seconds labelled 0.368, 0.135 and 0.050.
media.caption: Reference render of class F1.5 (design-system gallery). The data are synthetic and exist only to demonstrate the form.

source.note: Plot class from the design system's plot taxonomy; synthetic demonstration data. Standard theory only.

read_the_figure.question: How fast does it relax?
read_the_figure.axes: x: time t in seconds, 0 to 9. y: the signal, dimensionless, -1.2 to 1.5. Dashed amber curves are the envelope plus and minus exp(-t/tau) with tau = 1.5 s; pink markers sit on the envelope at t = tau, 2 tau, 3 tau.
look_at: How tall is the envelope after one, two and three time constants?
Do the peaks of the oscillation touch the envelope?
Is the oscillation period constant while the amplitude shrinks? Here it is about 1.05 s throughout.
At what time is the signal below 5 percent of its start? Read it from the 3 tau marker.
as_drawn: The envelope values are printed at the markers: 0.368, 0.135, 0.050, which are exp(-1), exp(-2), exp(-3).
The signal touches the envelope where cos(6t) = plus or minus 1. The first peak, at t = pi/3, sits on the dashed curve.
The note at top right states tau = 1.5 s and that the amplitude falls to 1/e per tau. y is linear, so the late decay is almost invisible.
read_the_figure.proves: That the amplitude decays exponentially with the stated time constant, at least at the three marked times. It does not prove the decay is exactly exponential at other times, or give the physical cause.
if_wrong: Envelope drawn by eye, not from the formula or the fitted peaks: tau is guesswork.
Linear y axis only: a tail that decays differently from an exponential is invisible after 3 tau.
No time-constant markers: 'fast' and 'slow' have no scale.

terms.meaning: The time for an exponential decay to fall by a factor of e, that is to about 37 percent of its value.
A curve that bounds the oscillation from outside and touches its peaks.
Decay at a rate proportional to the current value.
The time to halve: tau times the natural log of 2.
An oscillation whose amplitude shrinks because of friction or loss.

remember: Envelope and oscillation period are independent numbers.
On a semi-log axis the envelope is a straight line of slope -1/tau.

understand.title: Marks and encodings
understand.text: A solid line is the signal; two dashed lines are the envelope, a mirror pair. Pink dots with dotted drop lines mark times that are whole multiples of tau, and their printed values read the envelope height. The faint grey line is y = 0.

understand.title: Why this form answers the question
understand.text: Two different clocks are present: the fast oscillation and the slow decay. The envelope separates them: it hides the oscillation and shows only the amplitude history. The time constant tau is a single number that describes the whole decay, and the markers at tau, 2 tau, 3 tau give it a scale you can read on the axis.

understand.title: How it misleads
understand.text: On a linear y axis everything after about 3 tau is flat, so a slower tail would hide there. An envelope drawn through only a few peaks can mislead if the sampling is coarse: sampled peaks always read low. And exp(-t/tau) is a model; the figure cannot show that the real system follows it.

understand.title: Why each required item matters
understand.text: Tau markers turn a vague 'decays quickly' into a time. The envelope shows the amplitude law without the oscillation getting in the way. Printed values let a reader check the exponential without a ruler.

understand.title: Alternatives
understand.text: Plot the logarithm of the peak heights against time: an exponential becomes a straight line whose slope gives tau, and any deviation is easy to see. For a damped oscillator also report the damping ratio and the quality factor. A spectrogram is better when the decay rate changes with frequency.

understand.title: A variant to create
understand.text: Add a lower panel with ln of the envelope against t, with a fitted line and tau printed. Mark the half-life and the time to reach 5 percent on the time axis.

steps.title: Reading tau from two envelope points
steps.note: Using the printed markers: A(1.5) = 0.368 and A(3.0) = 0.135, ln(0.368 / 0.135) = 1.00, so tau = 1.5 / 1.00 = 1.5 s. Consistent with the label.

steps.title: Time to reach a fraction
steps.note: For 5 percent, t = 1.5 x ln 20 = 4.49 s (3.0 tau). For half, 1.04 s.

steps.title: Damped oscillator link
steps.note: The envelope's time constant is set by the damping ratio times the natural frequency.

worked.title: Reading the reference render
worked.problem: From the figure: (1) what fraction of the start amplitude remains at t = 4.5 s? (2) What is the oscillation period? (3) When has the signal dropped below 5 percent?

solution.text: The marker at 3 tau = 4.5 s is labelled 0.050: 5 percent.
Successive peaks of the teal curve are about 1.05 s apart.
The same 3 tau marker: about 4.5 s. Check:

worked.answer: 5 percent at 4.5 s, period 1.05 s: one time constant spans about 1.4 oscillation periods (tau / T = 1.43), so the system rings only a few times.

analyze.q: The oscillation period is 1.05 s but tau is 1.5 s. How many oscillations happen in one tau and why does it matter for calling the system lightly damped?
If the envelope were drawn from only every second peak, what would the error be?
analyze.hint: Peaks sampled coarsely sit below the true envelope.

analyze.q: What does the plot look like if the system is overdamped?

evaluate.q: Three time constants is often called 'settled'. When is 5 percent not good enough?
evaluate.hint: Compare with a tolerance of the application.

create: Draw the semi-log companion panel and read tau from its slope.
Make a figure comparing two systems with tau = 0.5 s and 1.5 s on the same axes.

checks.q: What fraction is left after two time constants?
An envelope reads 0.6 at t = 1 s and 0.2 at t = 3 s. What is tau?
The envelope passes through the three markers but the real signal's tail stays above it after 6 s. What do you conclude?
checks.hint: A linear axis hides small values.
checks.answer: The decay is not purely exponential. Plot on a semi-log axis to see the tail and fit it separately.
